title: Seven Deadly Fitness Sins: Lust
summary: In his 'fitness capital sins' series, NH discusses lust: sexual desire is a normal first motivation for lifting, but the deeper drive in bodybuilding is the male power fantasy of maximal muscularity. Lust becomes a sin when it distracts you from your goals or, once you believe the goal is out of reach, turns into bitterness aimed at others.

claims.claim: Wanting to be more attractive to the opposite sex (or the same sex) is a natural, biological reason many young men start lifting, and nothing is wrong with it.
Attraction should eventually stop being your number one goal; men who never move past it build an aesthetic physique (abs, pecs, arms) and often skip legs and upper back.
Most women don't want massive men; the physique most of them like (Brad Pitt in Fight Club) is easy for most men to reach, and stopping there stalls progression.
His goal is to get as big as his body naturally allows at the lowest bodyfat possible, which he sees as the pinnacle of masculinity.
Bodybuilding centres on admiring the male body; for the mostly straight bodybuilders the drive is a male power fantasy of being biggest and strongest, not sexual lust.
Most followers of big men on YouTube and Instagram are other men who aspire to become that image, which is achievable only if the image is natural.
Men who reach the physique they thought would get them laid, and don't, can feel intense frustration.
Always wanting more muscle is fine unless it damages your mental health through body dysmorphia.
Lust becomes a fitness sin when chasing sex or power distracts you from becoming the best you can be.
When someone decides the goal is out of reach, that lust can turn to bitterness and pain, often aimed at people who achieved what they wanted.
